chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Ibrahim ibn Umar al-Yamani, from Ismail ibn Abdul Khaliq, who said:

I was beside Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), and with him were his son Abdullah and the son who followed him. A man said to him, 'May Allah keep you well! Does a man perform Tawaf on behalf of another man who is residing in Mecca, with no illness preventing him?' He said, 'No. Had that been permissible, I would have ordered my so-and-so son to perform Tawaf on my behalf,' mentioning the younger one, and they were both listening.
ai.seo_question: Can a healthy person perform Tawaf on behalf of another healthy person in Mecca?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the specific conditions for *Tawaf al-Na’ib* (substitute circumambulation), ruling that it is not permissible for a healthy person to perform it for another healthy person merely residing in Mecca. By citing his own sons as examples, he emphasizes that the concession is strictly for cases of necessity or illness, thereby preventing the generalization of the practice to all pilgrims. This hadith is foundational in Shia jurisprudence for distinguishing between obligatory substitute acts and voluntary ones, reinforcing the principle that *Tawaf* is primarily a personal act of worship unless a valid excuse exists.
